artworks.title: Apollo and Daphne (marble, Galleria Borghese, Rome)
artworks.description: Bernini's Baroque marble catches Ovid's instant of change — bark closing over Daphne's flesh as Apollo's hand still grasps what is already becoming laurel. The Thessalian nymph of Peneus, not the Arcadian huntress of the Ladon, is the figure the poets crown with Apollo's tree.

artworks.title: Apollo and Daphne
artworks.description: A small early Renaissance panel in the National Gallery, London: Apollo pursues Daphne as laurel leaves already sprout from her raised hands. Pollaiuolo turns Ovid's metamorphosis into a courtly chase on a narrow stage — one of the first great painted statements of the nymph who becomes the poet's crown.

artworks.title: Apollo and Daphne
artworks.description: Waterhouse's late Pre-Raphaelite canvas freezes the flight at the riverbank: Daphne twists away as bark and foliage claim her limbs, Apollo still reaching. The Victorian classicist makes the nymph's terror and transformation the whole drama — desire checked by the green armour of the laurel.

artworks.title: Apollo in Love with Daphne
artworks.description: Poussin's unfinished late masterpiece in the Louvre gathers the whole Ovidian episode into a lucid classical landscape: Apollo pursues, Daphne flees toward her river-father, and the metamorphosis begins at the edge of the grove. It is among the last mythological inventions of the painter who taught Europe how to stage antiquity with quiet geometry.

artworks.title: Apollo and Daphne
artworks.description: Tiepolo's Rococo oil lightens the chase into Venetian air and colour: Apollo lunges as Daphne's fingers leaf into laurel. Where Bernini carved panic in marble, Tiepolo paints the same Ovidian instant as luminous theatre — the nymph's escape staged for an eighteenth-century ceiling imagination.

music.title: Dafne
music.description: Peri's Dafne is often called the first opera — Daphne's flight from Apollo as the newborn art form's founding subject.

music.title: Daphne
music.description: Strauss's bucolic tragedy for Dresden ends in the metamorphosis itself — Daphne's voice dissolving into the shimmering strings of the laurel tree.

popCulture.title: Poet laureate
popCulture.description: The laurel crown that names a poet laureate is Daphne's tree — Apollo's prize after the nymph escaped him as bark and leaf.

popCulture.title: Daphne
popCulture.description: Daphne endures as the laurel of poetry itself — the nymph who became the crown Apollo still wears.
